title: WHY DID FIVE BRIDESMAIDS RUN OUT OF OIL? THE TERRIFYING NIGHT WHEN THE DOOR CLOSED
paragraphs: WHY DID FIVE BRIDESMAIDS RUN OUT OF OIL? THE TERRIFYING NIGHT WHEN THE DOOR CLOSED

They had the lamps. They received the invitation. They waited for the Bridegroom. But when midnight came, five discovered that looking ready was not the same as being ready. And the most frightening words in the story were spoken by the One they thought they knew.
There is something deeply unsettling about a door that closes while someone is still begging to come inside.
Especially when the person knocking was invited.
Especially when they had spent the entire night waiting.
Especially when they believed they belonged at the celebration.
Now imagine standing outside that door, hearing the celebration begin without you.
You knock.
Nothing.
You knock again.
Then a voice answers from the other side.
“Verily I say unto you, I know you not.” — Matthew 25:12 (KJV)
Read those words again.
Not because Jesus enjoys frightening people.
But because He loves us enough to warn us before the door closes.

This is the parable of the ten virgins, often described as ten bridesmaids, in Matthew 25:1–13. And although Christians have heard it preached countless times, there is a detail many of us have overlooked.
All ten were waiting for the same Bridegroom.
All ten carried lamps.
All ten expected the wedding.
All ten became drowsy.
All ten fell asleep.
But only five were prepared when the moment finally arrived.
What separated them was not how impressive they appeared before midnight.
It was what their preparation revealed when midnight came.
And that should make every one of us examine our hearts.
Because it is possible to spend years surrounded by Christian things and still neglect the most important question of all.
Do I truly belong to Jesus Christ?
Jesus begins the story by describing ten young women who took their lamps and went out to meet a bridegroom.
Five were wise.
Five were foolish.
The Greek words Matthew uses are worth examining.
The wise are called φρόνιμοι (phronimoi), meaning prudent, sensible, or discerning.
The foolish are called μωραί (mōrai), meaning foolish or lacking sound judgment.
Jesus was not describing five intelligent women and five women who struggled academically.
He was exposing the difference between people who acted wisely in light of what they knew and people who failed to prepare for what they knew could happen.
The foolish bridesmaids were not condemned because they did not know a wedding was coming.
They knew.
They simply failed to prepare adequately for the possibility of a delay.
Matthew 25:3–4 says:
“They that were foolish took their lamps, and took no oil with them: But the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps.” (KJV)
Notice something important.
The foolish bridesmaids apparently had lamps that could burn for a time. Later, they cried that their lamps were going out.
Their problem was not necessarily that they had never possessed a drop of oil.
Their problem was that they had not brought the additional supply needed for the wait.
They prepared for an arrival.
But they did not prepare for a delay.
And suddenly, this ancient story begins to sound painfully familiar.
Because some people are enthusiastic about Jesus when life is exciting.
When the worship music is powerful.
When prayers are answered quickly.
When the church is full.
When the testimony is beautiful.
When faith feels effortless.
But what happens when the healing does not come immediately?
When the marriage is breaking apart?
When the financial burden grows heavier?
When the temptation returns?
When the grief lasts longer than anyone expected?
When God seems silent, even though His promises remain true?
What happens when following Jesus becomes costly, lonely, or inconvenient?
A faith built only for exciting moments may struggle when obedience requires endurance.
And yet we must be careful here.
Jesus never explicitly says that the oil represents the Holy Spirit, good works, prayer, or any single spiritual discipline.
Throughout Scripture, oil can be associated with anointing, consecration, and other purposes. But Matthew 25 does not provide a direct interpretation of the oil as one particular thing.
The central emphasis of the parable is readiness for the Bridegroom's arrival.
That readiness cannot be borrowed at the last minute.
It cannot be replaced by religious appearances.
And it cannot be postponed indefinitely.
The oil matters because it exposes who was prepared.
And the Bridegroom matters because the entire story revolves around His coming.
Then Jesus introduces a detail that changes the atmosphere.
“While the bridegroom tarried, they all slumbered and slept.” — Matthew 25:5 (KJV)
They all slept.
Not just the foolish.
The wise slept too.
That distinction matters.
Jesus does not present the wise bridesmaids as superhuman believers who never became physically tired.
Nor does He identify ordinary sleep as their spiritual failure.
The contrast is not between those who slept and those who stayed awake.
It is between those who were prepared for the delay and those who were not.
The wise had made provision before the unexpected moment arrived.
The foolish had not.
And then, at midnight, the silence shattered.
“Behold, the bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet him.” — Matthew 25:6 (KJV)
Midnight.
The hour when everything seemed quiet.
The hour when no one could pretend the wait had not been long.
The hour when preparation was finally tested.
Picture the scene.
Ten women suddenly rising.
Hands reaching for lamps.
Flames being tended.
The distant excitement of an approaching wedding procession.
Five women discovering that their lamps could continue burning.
And five realizing, with mounting horror, that theirs were going out.
Imagine one of them staring into her lamp.
Perhaps she had carried it proudly earlier that evening.
Perhaps it looked no different from the others.
Perhaps no one could have recognized the problem until that moment.
But now the flame was fading.
And the Bridegroom was coming.
The foolish turned to the wise and pleaded:
“Give us of your oil; for our lamps are gone out.” — Matthew 25:8 (KJV)
It was a desperate request.
And humanly speaking, it was understandable.
But the wise replied that there would not be enough for everyone and instructed them to go purchase oil.
This is not a lesson encouraging Christians to refuse generosity.
The wise bridesmaids were not praised for selfishness.
The point is that their supply could not be divided without jeopardizing the readiness of everyone.
The story presses toward a sobering truth.
Some things cannot be transferred from one person to another.
Your mother can pray for you.
Your father can teach you Scripture.
Your pastor can proclaim the Gospel.
Your spouse can encourage you toward repentance.
Your friends can walk beside you through spiritual battles.
But none of them can repent on your behalf.
None can personally trust Christ in your place.
None can possess a saving relationship with Jesus for you.
You cannot inherit salvation merely because your family is Christian.
You cannot borrow another person's faith because you attend the same church.
You cannot substitute public religious activity for personal trust in the Savior.
Salvation is God's gift of grace, received through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (KJV)
And verse 10 immediately teaches that those saved by grace are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Works are not the price of salvation.
They are part of the transformed life God produces in those who belong to Him.
That is why this parable should never be twisted into a message that says, “Perform enough religious activities and Jesus will finally accept you.”
The Gospel says something far more beautiful.
Jesus Christ came to save sinners who could never save themselves.
He lived in perfect obedience.
He died for sins.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith finds mercy in the Savior who is mighty to save.
But the same grace that forgives us also calls us to follow Him.
Not to earn His love.
But because His love changes us.
And this is where the story becomes deeply personal.
There are people who know the language of Christianity without having surrendered their hearts to Christ.
They know when to say “Amen.”
They know the songs.
They know the familiar Bible verses.
They may even know how to sound spiritually mature in front of others.
But behind closed doors, they are exhausted from maintaining an image.
Some are hiding sins they refuse to confront.
Some have quietly drifted away from prayer and Scripture.
Some have confused church attendance with genuine discipleship.
Others genuinely love Jesus but are so wounded, ashamed, or spiritually weary that they fear their struggles mean God has abandoned them.
If that is you, please hear the difference.
Struggling does not automatically mean you are pretending.
A bruised believer who keeps turning toward Jesus is not the same as a person who deliberately rejects Him while relying on religious appearances.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
His failure was real.
His grief was real.
But his story did not end beside that charcoal fire of denial.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and called him to follow Him.
That is grace.
Not permission to remain in sin.
Not a promise that repentance is unnecessary.
But mercy powerful enough to meet a broken sinner and begin restoring what sin has devastated.
Perhaps you are reading this with memories you wish you could erase.
A relationship you damaged.
A promise you broke.
A secret you have hidden.
A season when you walked away from God.
And somewhere in your heart, you wonder whether Jesus could still receive you.
Listen to His own words.
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37 (KJV)
There is your invitation.
Not an invitation to pretend.
An invitation to come.
Not to purchase acceptance.
But to receive mercy from the One who gave Himself for sinners.
The tragedy of the five foolish bridesmaids is not that the Bridegroom was unwilling to celebrate a wedding.
The tragedy is that they were unprepared when the appointed moment arrived.
Matthew tells us:
“And while they went to buy, the bridegroom came; and they that were ready went in with him to the marriage: and the door was shut.” — Matthew 25:10 (KJV)
Four words.
“And the door was shut.”
No dramatic speech.
No extended explanation.
Just a door.
Closed.
The women who were ready entered the celebration.
Those who had gone to purchase oil were absent when the Bridegroom arrived.
And when they returned, they cried:
“Lord, Lord, open to us.” — Matthew 25:11 (KJV)
In Greek, their plea begins:
Κύριε κύριε, ἄνοιξον ἡμῖν.
Kyrie, kyrie, anoixon hēmin.
“Lord, Lord, open to us.”
The repetition carries urgency.
They were not asking casually.
They were pleading.
And the answer is devastating.
“Verily I say unto you, I know you not.” — Matthew 25:12 (KJV)
The Greek reads:
ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, οὐκ οἶδα ὑμᾶς.
Amēn legō hymin, ouk oida hymas.
“Truly I say to you, I do not know you.”
The expression communicates a refusal to recognize them as belonging within the wedding celebration.
It echoes another warning Jesus gave in Matthew 7:21–23, where merely calling Him “Lord” is shown to be insufficient apart from a genuine relationship with Him.
This does not mean God lacks information about anyone.
God knows all things.
The issue is recognition, belonging, and relationship.
And that makes the warning even more serious.
Because the question is not merely whether we know facts about Jesus.
The question is whether we truly belong to Him.
Not whether we can impress people with our Christianity.
Not whether we have accumulated enough religious achievements.
Not whether we can recite the right words while refusing to trust and obey Him.
But whether our hope rests in the crucified and risen Christ.
And now consider the original setting.
Jesus spoke this parable during His teaching about His future coming.
In Matthew 24, He warned His disciples that the timing of His return would be unexpected and that they must remain ready.
Then, in Matthew 25, He told the story of the bridesmaids.
The concluding command is unmistakable:
“Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour wherein the Son of man cometh.” — Matthew 25:13 (KJV)
The Greek imperative is γρηγορεῖτε (grēgoreite).
It means “keep watch” or “stay alert.”
But because all ten bridesmaids slept, Jesus is not commanding literal sleeplessness.
He is calling for continuing spiritual readiness.
The Christian life is not supposed to be a frantic attempt to predict the date of Christ's return.
Jesus does not tell His followers to calculate the hour.
He tells them to be ready.
And being ready begins with belonging to Him.
Not with fear-driven performance.
Not with purchasing religious security.
Not with comparing ourselves to other believers.
But with repentance, faith, and a life increasingly shaped by His grace.
There is another word worth remembering.
The Hebrew Scriptures frequently use שׁוּב (shuv) for turning or returning.
It is a powerful word in passages calling God's people to turn away from evil and return to Him.
And the New Testament calls people to repentance through words such as μετανοέω (metanoeō), meaning to repent or change one's mind in a way that involves turning from sin toward God.
The languages are different, and the words are not identical in every nuance.
But together they illuminate a deeply biblical invitation.
Turn.
Return.
Come to the Lord.
Do not wait until your heart feels impressive.
Do not wait until you have fixed every consequence of your past.
Do not wait until you can present a version of yourself that no longer needs mercy.
Come to Jesus because you need mercy.
And if you already belong to Him but have grown spiritually careless, return to the practices that help you walk closely with Him.
Open your Bible again.
Pray honestly again.
Confess the sin you have been defending.
Seek reconciliation where possible.
Find fellowship with believers who will speak truth in love.
Serve others without needing applause.
Persevere when following Christ becomes difficult.
None of these actions can purchase salvation.
But they belong within the life of discipleship to which Jesus calls His people.
And please understand something else.
The five wise bridesmaids were not invited into the celebration because they possessed extraordinary lamps.
They were ready for the Bridegroom.
The Bridegroom was the center of the story.
And Jesus Christ must remain the center of ours.
Not our spiritual reputation.
Not our ministries.
Not our platforms.
Not our accomplishments.
Not even the intensity of our emotions while reading an article like this.
Jesus.
Always Jesus.
The One who was rejected so that sinners could be reconciled to God.
The One who bore our sins on the cross.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who will come again.
The One whose grace does not merely cover a scandalous past but begins transforming the person who brings that past to Him.
From scandal to grace is not a story about sinners becoming impressive. It is a story about Jesus being a magnificent Savior.
And perhaps that is the part you needed to hear most.
Because someone reading this has spent years believing their worst chapter is the final chapter.
You remember the betrayal.
The addiction.
The dishonesty.
The compromise.
The bitterness.
The prayers you stopped praying because you felt too ashamed to approach God.
You have wondered whether you have wandered too far.
But the Gospel still announces that forgiveness is found in Jesus Christ.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
That promise does not encourage us to hide our sins.
It gives us courage to bring them into the light.
And if this story has exposed something in your heart, you do not need to manufacture an emotional experience to prove your sincerity.
You can speak to God honestly, right where you are.

“Lord Jesus, I have spent too much time looking ready instead of examining whether I am truly walking with You. Forgive my sins. Strip away my pride, my excuses, and my religious pretending. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. I place my trust in You, not in my ability to save myself. Teach me to repent, obey, endure, and love You with a sincere heart. And when the waiting becomes difficult, remind me that Your promises are trustworthy. Amen.”
A prayer is not a magical formula.
The words themselves do not save.
Jesus saves.
But if those words reflect the genuine turning of your heart toward Him, do not dismiss the importance of that response.
And do not keep it isolated from a life of discipleship.
Find a faithful local church.
Learn the Scriptures.
Seek baptism if you have not been baptized as a believer, in keeping with your church's biblical understanding and practice.
Walk with mature Christians.
Continue growing.
Because following Jesus is not merely about experiencing one emotional moment.
It is about belonging to Him throughout the journey.
And that journey is one reason Gospel Warrior exists.
There are people opening their phones at midnight who are not looking for entertainment.
They are searching for hope.
A father quietly overwhelmed by responsibilities.
A mother crying after everyone else has fallen asleep.
A young person battling temptation and shame.
A believer struggling to return after years of spiritual distance.
Someone who has never understood why the cross matters.
Someone who needs to hear, perhaps for the first time, that Jesus Christ receives repentant sinners.
Every Scripture-centered article, devotional, and discipleship resource is an opportunity to place biblical truth before someone who may desperately need it.
And if this message has helped you, I want to invite you to become part of that mission.
And certainly not because a monthly payment replaces your responsibility to worship, serve, and give faithfully according to Scripture.
But voluntary financial support can be a genuine expression of Christian generosity and stewardship when it is given freely, responsibly, and with a sincere desire to serve others.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be done reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is a meaningful way to participate in a mission beyond yourself.
Those products are not the heart of this mission.
Jesus Christ is.
But they can serve as reminders of biblical truth, encouragement for everyday life, and thoughtful gifts that open conversations about faith.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your faithful sharing of biblical truth matters.
You can help someone encounter this message without spending anything.
Give, if you choose to give, not out of guilt or fear but out of love for God and neighbor.
Not simply to increase a number on a screen.
But because somewhere among your friends and family, someone may be waiting for a reminder that the door of mercy is open today.
Someone may have a Bible collecting dust beside their bed.
Someone may have grown comfortable with the appearance of faith while neglecting its reality.
Someone may be frightened that their past has disqualified them from receiving grace.
Someone may need both the warning and the invitation found in this parable.
And please, do not leave this message as something you merely read and forget.
Return to Matthew 25:1–13.
Read the entire passage in its context.
Examine your heart before God.
Or share a testimony of how Jesus has been restoring your life.
You do not need to reveal private sins or painful details publicly. Genuine repentance begins before God, and wise support can also happen through trusted, confidential relationships.
But sometimes one honest testimony reminds another struggling believer that grace is real.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling Christians, people exploring the faith, and those who have drifted from church to follow as well.
Not because a social media page can replace the body of Christ.
But because truth shared through ordinary places can become an invitation to open the Bible, seek a faithful church, and draw nearer to Jesus.
The Bridegroom has arrived.
The celebration is beginning.
Five bridesmaids are inside.
Five are outside.
And the story has become terribly quiet.
There is no indication that the foolish bridesmaids hated the Bridegroom.
No indication that they opposed the wedding.
No indication that they wanted the celebration canceled.
They wanted to be there.
But wanting to be present was not the same as being prepared.
That is what makes this warning so searching.
It is possible to desire the benefits associated with Jesus while resisting the surrender involved in following Him.
It is possible to admire His teachings without trusting Him as Savior.
It is possible to be fascinated by prophecy while neglecting the ordinary obedience of today.
And it is possible to spend so much time asking when Christ will return that we forget to ask whether we are living in readiness for His return.
But do not leave this parable thinking Jesus is asking you to save yourself by collecting enough spiritual oil.
He is calling you to take His coming seriously.
To abandon false confidence.
To receive His grace.
To follow Him faithfully.
To live ready, not because you know the hour, but because you know the Savior.
Today, the Gospel invitation is still being proclaimed.
Today, sinners are still being called to repentance and faith.
Today, weary believers can return to the Lord.
Today, there is reason to seek Him rather than postpone the question until tomorrow.
Hebrews 3:15 declares:
“To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts.” (KJV)
The five bridesmaids ran out of oil because they had not prepared adequately for the Bridegroom's delayed arrival.
But Jesus told the story because He wanted His hearers to understand something far greater than the contents of a lamp.
The coming of the Son of Man is certain.
Its timing is unknown to us.
And readiness cannot be faked when the decisive moment arrives.
So come to Christ.
Trust Him.
Follow Him.
And let His grace transform the life you once thought could never be redeemed.
Because the greatest tragedy is not that midnight comes unexpectedly, but that someone hears the invitation to grace today and keeps postponing their answer.
